posts.title: Meet the herd: Biscuit, Maple, Cowboy and Captain Carrot

content.text: Every horse in our therapy herd is chosen for temperament, then trained for therapy. Children quickly learn their names, moods and favorite treats.

Biscuit is steady and patient, often paired with a child's first session. Maple is gentle and attentive. Cowboy brings a calm confidence to the arena, and Captain Carrot is endlessly food-motivated — which makes him an excellent teacher of routine and responsibility.
Children quickly learn their names, moods and favorite treats.

posts.title: What a session in the arena actually looks like

content.text: Sessions happen in the clinic and in the arena with our small therapy herd. For many families, the arena is the part they picture least clearly before their first visit.
Clinical goals, not just a horse ride

A session is built around the same clinical goals as any other therapy visit — gait, sensory processing, communication, confidence — with the horse as the motivating partner, not the point of the visit.

items: A licensed therapist leads every session
Goals are set and tracked the same as in-clinic care
Horses are matched to each child's needs and comfort level

posts.title: Five ways equine-assisted learning helps kids build confidence

content.text: Equine-assisted learning asks a child to communicate clearly, stay calm, and build trust with a thousand-pound animal that responds honestly to how they show up. That combination teaches things a worksheet cannot.

items: Reading and responding to nonverbal cues
Follow-through on a task from start to finish
Confidence that carries over outside the arena
